scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The imported Amuwu polygon is coastal Santa Barbara County and covers 1492 to 1500. The cited detailed evidence concerns the Chumash rancheria at the relocated Mission La Purísima, principally 1813 to 1848. No claim is made that the map is a verified fifteenth-century state boundary or that the mission created the people.

The earlier mission and the 1813 relocation are distinguished. The later mission place name is attested in the cited scholarship and community language discussion; these sources do not establish a precise pre-1813 settlement history at the excavated buildings.

The nomination was consulted for relocation, work and the water system. Its draft and final versions count as one work. Reconstructed park structures are distinguished from surviving historical fabric.

The 2021 food and economy paper was read in author-posted full text. Archaeological observations, regional comparisons and model-based estimates are distinguished. No calculated number of beads is presented as a literal excavated count. The floor-tile hoofprint does not prove indoor husbandry.

The 2023 housing paper and 2024 cache paper were read through their public publisher abstracts, not subscription full texts. The card limits its claims accordingly. Online publication occurred in 2022 and 2023 respectively.

The northern refuse deposit supports a suggested tule-house area, not directly observed complete houses. Status interpretation does not equate European objects with European ethnicity or with a single measure of cultural loss.
The cache study proposes alternative prominent Indigenous occupants. The card names no individual as its proven owner and does not identify exact vessel types unavailable in the abstract.

The 2024 public archaeology paper was read for community collaboration, place naming, material work and terminology. A photographed object is described through the paper; no claim is made to have independently examined the object.

California State Parks dates the recapture to March 17, 1824, under Mexican rule. Its history supports the 1845 grant to Elceario and Pastor Choyama. Secularization is not treated as ethnic extinction.
The 1834 to 1846 phase brackets the narrative events, not an asserted final year of occupation. No unsupported conquest or successor link is added.
Independent historical review, identity and border verification, and depth certification remain pending.
